questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was crucial to me to find a place with high academic level and international staff to both expand my professional skills but also experience the different culture. I also highly valued that I could meet the place before agreeing to go there.

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Very difficult. I lived in an airbnb for the first month trying to find something, was subjected to a scam, and then finally found an apartment that however was way too expensive, but this was the only option I had. I would recommend finding something ahead of arrival and make sure to get a live meeting with the landlord to see the apartment, because there are MANY scams in Bologna, and all students struggle with finding a place to live. Start looking ahead of arrival. The ideal scenario would be yo go there yourself and meet the people that rent out the apartment, so you know they and the apartment exist.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Be aware of all the scams! It is easiest to find a place with other students, so look through facebook groups, but again, be aware of scammers. If you know anybody in the city (like your supervisor or other students) ask them to check out the apartment. Also, it is easiest if you know the national language or bring someone who does.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were very poor possibilities in Bologna. Almost all place have the "4+4", which means that they only rent for at least 4 years. And most agencies don't lent to students. The opportunities were thus very limited, and it would definitely have been useful with some help for this proces. The options through the university were there, but VERY expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The Erasmus network is very well-organized in Bologna, and there are a broad array of opportunities from various sports (volley, football, running, yoga etc.), cultural activities (pubcrawl, city tours, pasta courses), and trips (beach trips, weekend trips to nearby cities, ski trips).

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I did not attend a lot, but from what I've heard, most of them worked out really good, and a lot of people go on the trips, and I think it is a great opportunity to meet other exchange students and create a social life in the city.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go on trips to other cities. Bologna has a huge train station and i centrally localized, so that all trains pass through Bologna. In this way you can get anywhere really fast. Further, domestic flights are quite cheap if you want to go to the very south of Italy, it might me easier and faster if just for a weekend. I would highly recommend visiting Cinque Terre, Naples, Rome, Milan, and also just for a trip to the beach since this is a 1,5 hour trip with train. In Bologna, I would take a course in FICO Eataly World, where theres both wine tastings, pasta courses, mortadella courses etc. which is a nice experience. I would also recommend go hiking. Mountains are just outside Bologna and are very beautiful for watching sunsets and picnics, and the famous Via Degli Dei (rout of Gods) is a hike from the center of Bologna to Florence (so a 4-7 day hiking trip). Finally, take the time to stand in line to eat at "Sfoglia Rina", it is very very good pasta.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was fine. Italy is not that different, however not all Italians outside of the university understand or speak English, so knowing some basic phrases is very nice. Further, Italians are not very strict about times, so they're often late by 10-60 minutes, so this is something I should get used to.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I would definitely take some italian courses, Babbel is a great platform to do so, even though it cost a bit, I think it is worth it. Italians love when other people try to learn their language and are happy to help! I would also sign up for the social stuff through the Erasmus network to get to know people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The only big difference is the language. It is very difficult to socialize with the locals, and they're not always so good at switching to english, when international people are around. This could sometimes make me feel a bit lonely. However, I did not take any courses at the university, so this experience is solely from the research group I was in.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed the aperitivo concept of grapping a drink or beer after work/school. The entire city does this, which means that from 16-18 there's people siting outside at every bar having a drink. It is just a very nice energy and atmosphere in the city and I really enjoyed this concept instead of going directly home every day.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
I would definitely take Italian courses before going! It just give a way better understanding. 
I would also seek help to find a place to live. If possible, go there yourself to make sure to avoid scammers. If you know someone in Bologna, or somebody who speaks Italian, make them help you, as not everybody understand English.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I think most of it has already been mentioned.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed living in Bologna, and it was very rewarding to try to live abroad in general, but I also think Bologna is perfect for this. I also tried to live with roomies which I have never done before, and I think this was a very great experience.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It was very mentally challenging to be social. As I didn't take any courses but only did my master's thesis in a research group, I was surrounded by the same people all the time. These people were not very good at talking English when I was around, which made me feel quite lonely some times. Also I think doing a master's thesis abroad in general is a challenge, and I had troubles identifying the guidelines since my Italian and Danish supervisor had never talked, and therefore I was guided in different directions which were a big problem.
